opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because people often assume generative AI only makes responsible AI harder, and in a lot of ways it does. The risks are broader, the outputs are open-ended, and you can't just look at one accuracy number and call it done. But it has also given us some powerful new tools on the safety side.

The biggest shift for me is in testing. With traditional machine learning, a lot of responsible AI work was bottlenecked on data. If you wanted to check whether a system behaved fairly across groups, or held up in unusual situations, you had to collect and label examples by hand, and that was slow and expensive. Often the coverage just wasn't there. Now we can use generative models to help create test data at scale. We can simulate adversarial users, generate many variations of a risky prompt, and probe a system the way a red teamer would, but across far more scenarios than a human team could cover alone.

The second piece is measurement. Many of the harms we care about, like whether a response is ungrounded, contains harmful content, or leaks something it shouldn't, used to require human judgment to evaluate. With careful design and validation against human labels, we can use models as evaluators. That lets us run measurements continuously, every time we change a prompt or update a model, rather than as a one-off review at the end. That moves responsible AI from a checkpoint to part of the everyday engineering loop.

And third, these same capabilities power mitigations. Classifiers for content safety, prompt shields that detect jailbreak or injection attempts, and groundedness detection are all built on the same advances.

So I see it as a real step forward. The technology that creates new risks also gives us the ability to find, measure, and manage those risks much more systematically. Humans still need to be in the loop, defining what "good" looks like, red teaming creatively, and checking that the automated evaluators are trustworthy. But we can now do this work at the speed and scale the technology demands, which wasn't possible before.

r001.rationale: The response says models can evaluate harms with careful design and validation against human labels, but does not state that their safety scoring is comparable to expert human linguists.

r002.rationale: It says continuous measurement moves responsible AI from a final checkpoint into the everyday engineering loop, including when prompts or models are updated.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's interesting because a lot of people's first reaction to generative AI is that it makes responsible AI harder, and in some ways that's true. The surface area is bigger, the outputs are open-ended, the same model can be used for a thousand different things. But what I've actually found is that it's been a huge step forward for how we test and evaluate systems, and I'd point to a couple of reasons for that.

The first is that generative AI gives us a much better tool for generating test cases. Historically, if you wanted to evaluate a system for something like fairness or harmful content, you had to painstakingly hand-build a dataset. You'd have people write examples, you'd try to cover all the different categories of harm, all the different ways someone might phrase a prompt, and it was slow and expensive and you never really got the coverage you wanted. Now we can use models to simulate an adversarial user and generate thousands of variations of attacks across different harm categories and different styles. So our red teaming has gone from being almost entirely manual to being something we can scale and run continuously, every time the system changes.

The second piece is on the evaluation side. A lot of the things we care about are inherently fuzzy. Is this response grounded in the source documents? Is it appropriately refusing, or is it over-refusing? Is this content actually harmful in context? Those don't reduce to a simple string match, and before you really needed humans in the loop to judge them. Now we can use models as evaluators, with a lot of care around calibrating them against human judgments, and that lets us measure quality and safety at a scale that just wasn't possible before.

And then the third thing, which I think is maybe underappreciated, is that generative AI forced the whole industry to take this seriously at the same time. When ChatGPT and Bing Chat came out, suddenly every team building a product had to think about what happens when the model says something it shouldn't. That created a lot of demand for tooling and for shared practices, and it meant responsible AI stopped being a niche thing that a small group did on the side and became part of the core engineering process. So the risks are real, and I don't want to minimize them, but from a testing and measurement standpoint, I actually think we're in a much stronger position than we were a few years ago.

r001.rationale: The candidate says models can evaluate fuzzy safety questions at scale when calibrated against human judgments, but does not state that automated safety scoring is comparable to expert human linguists.

r002.rationale: The candidate says red teaming can run continuously every time the system changes and that responsible AI has become part of the core engineering process, communicating testing within the development loop.

astra-6.text:
I think generative AI gives us an opportunity to make responsible AI testing much more comprehensive. Traditionally, a lot of testing has depended on people anticipating what might go wrong, creating examples, and then manually evaluating how a system responds. That work is essential, but it’s difficult to scale.

With generative AI, we can use AI to help test AI—to generate challenging inputs, explore variations on a scenario, and help identify responses that need closer review. That lets us investigate a broader range of potential failures and repeat those tests as we improve the system.

It doesn’t eliminate the need for human judgment. People still need to define what safety means in a particular context and check whether our evaluations actually capture it. But it can give those people much better tools, making testing a more continuous part of development.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating challenging inputs and flagging responses for human review, but does not state that generative AI can automate safety scoring or match expert human linguists.

r002.rationale: It says testing can become “a more continuous part of development,” conveying that it moves into the application development loop.

sol-6.1.text:
Generative AI gives us new ways to test systems, as well as new things we need to test. In the past, responsible AI testing often depended on people anticipating failure modes and manually building datasets to measure them. That’s important work, but it’s difficult to cover the range of situations a system might encounter.

Now we can use AI to help generate challenging inputs, explore variations, and simulate adversarial interactions. That lets us test more broadly and repeatedly as we improve a model or application.

The key is that AI helps scale the process; it doesn’t replace human judgment. We still need people to define what safe behavior means in a particular context, check whether our evaluations are meaningful, and investigate the failures. But we have a much more powerful tool for finding problems earlier and measuring whether our mitigations actually work.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI-generated test inputs and broader evaluation, but does not mention automated safety scoring comparable to expert human linguists.

r002.rationale: The response says testing can be repeated as a model or application improves, which suggests iterative development testing. It does not communicate the shift from final application validation into the development loop.
